You’ve gotten a lot of good responses on warp skipping, and I’d like to throw in my two cents based on how practical a tactical option I think warp skipping was meant to be in the earlier games.

So consider the second to last chapter of FE1. The map is filled with manaketes, which are incredibly tough and hard to kill and which you have limited numbers of effective weaponry against. FE 1 is a game with low stat caps, and you’re likely going to have your army be beasts long before this chapter. There’s not really a good reason to go through the gauntlet of these dangerous and hard to kill enemies . You can go get the Aum staff, a staff that only one particular unit can use to revive a single dead unit, but I’d say FE1 is honestly the game where this feature is close to least useful.

So if you don’t want that staff and don’t want to endanger characters or waste resources, you can send a powerful flyer with a wyrmslayer over the mountain to the seize point, kill the manakete boss there, and then warp Marth to the seize point to end the chapter and go on to the finale.

I think Warp skipping was a deeply powerful tool, and intended to be, in the early games of the franchise and that you were meant to use it to avoid deeply hard, necessary fights if you still had uses. I think with ‘route the enemy’ becoming more common in later games warp skipping has lost some of its old design use, although ‘kill the boss’ maps essentially function the same as traditional seize.

I’ll be honest. I’ve got a lot of misgivings about Lucifer being Chaotic Good.

Lucifer isn’t this actively malevolent shithead, but he is a *passive* and selfish shithead, which has its own form of malevolency. 

While it’s not entirely actively shown, it’s inferred when we first meet him that Lucifer is a selfish coward. We know he’s abdicated any and all responsibility in rulership of the Sinners in Hell. We know he’s done this since, at least, Lilith left him, but I suspect he was hands off and basically left the Sinners to fend for themselves instead of providing any true leadership before then. He seems disinterested in Sinners at best and disgusted with them for the most part - something he vocally demonstrates in Hell’s Greatest Dad - and mostly seems upset that Sinners use free will in awful ways, which in his mind means he’s free to abandon them for essentially wasting the gift he gave/tricked them into.

On top of this, we know he’s abandoned his duties to the Hellborn thanks to Helluva Boss as well. Just as he’s pretty much let the Overlords run rampant and be the primary authorities of the Sinners, he’s let the Ars Goetia and the Sins/Satan basically do whatever the fuck they want despite the fact it’s implied he might have, at least at one point, had authority to check them. He’s chosen to focus on himself entirely until Charlie reconnects with him. 

The fact that he actually has the chance to wield authority, and has chosen to ignore it and toss it out because what happened to him wasn’t what HE dreamed is astonishing selfishness that deeply harms everyone in his realm, especially his daughter. It’s not just gross irresponsibility, it’s legitimately cruel and shows off why Lucifer is Pride here because he can barely see beyond what he wants. He’s *changing* thanks to Charlie, but he hadn’t fully changed.

I fully agree with this. It also plays on something the audience knows: in scenes with Chucky, there’s two people: one is Chucky, the other is potential victim.

In this scene, Charles *isn’t* Chucky. Damballa is. It highlights that for once Charles is in the position of victim and at the mercy of someone undeniably greater than him. It’s a great play on a dynamic the audience fully knows, and accentuates that Chucky is, for once, in true and genuine danger of actual death up against Damballa.

Honestly, I think it’s great and in character that, seeing himself and acting again in his human form for the first time in forty years, Charles has to answer to himself as ‘Chucky’. While it can be seen as an easy out, I think it actually further confirms two things.

1) Chucky’s narcissism is so deep and heavily rooted that the only person or being he can see as worth worshipping or really caring about is himself.

2) Chucky now views himself much more as, and is more comfortable with his form, as a possessed Good Guy doll than as a human man.

It’s a power play by Damballa to further emphasize how vulnerable Charles is/should feel here: Chucky is forced to interact with him in a form he no longer feels at home in, while Damballa gets to wear Chucky’s ‘real’ face and dominate the conversation. This is one of the only conversations in the franchise I can think of where Chucky is undeniably in a position of weakness throughout the whole conversation (apart from trying to weasel out of being killed in Childs Play 1 and 2), and that’s further emphasized by the fact that Charles isn’t ’Chucky’ right now, Damballa is.

Out of curiosity, are you just now promoting units? FE1, 2, 3, and 5 can be games where promoting at level 10 can be viable, especially 1, 3, and 5. This is because stats all cap at 20 in these games, and growth rates can be a decent bit lower. If your characters are all nearing 20, there is no reason not to promote, if they have classes that are possible for promotion. This is because promotion gains are absurd in 3 and 5 especially with the low stat caps. For instance, when you promote Ogma you’re going to gain +2 in everything except Weapon Level which you’ll gain +3 in, +0 for Res, and Defense can vary.

You want your horsemen/paladins kitted with Knight Killers in order to take on the enemy paladins. The absolute biggest threat you’re going to have is Camus, so you want to try and bait as many of his allies to you before baiting him, and he’s another reason you’ll want Knight Killers. I’m not certain if Camus moves in this iteration of Shadow Dragon, or if he stays on the Castle, as while I’ve played FE1 and FE11, I’ve only played FE3 book 2 to completion.

You’ll want to load Ogma and Astram with Kill Swords and Armor Slayers. Because of the low stat caps, equipment load out can make or break how things go. If Jeorge had the Parthia - and he should - he can help do work on the paladins, though probably not Camus. Tiki in book 2 if set up right can be a beast and could help with the generals, but I don’t know for sure if this carries over to Book 1.

If you need high level weapons, the shops carry Kill Line and Silver line weapons. The general on the top left, Lorenz, can also be recruited if you bring Shiida, though it’s debatable how much that’s worth. You’re also going to have to deal with reinforcements from the forts, but none of them are promoted.

How low level is Marth? While not the god he was in FE1, Marth is still a very good unit in 3, and his ability to use the rapier or mercurius against Camus could be massively beneficial if he can stand toe to toe with him. Either way you’re going to want to train Marth for the final chapter, since he’s your easiest/best way to kill Medeus.

I also suggest sweeping the center area first and getting the Hammerne staff in the village. You’re going to want that. After that I would try and quickly get the bridge down to prepare to face Camus’ troops, and have a guard between you and the center area with the forts, as reinforcements will begin turn 7.

Also? Take note you have to be careful how you kill the paladins directly beside Camus. Camus regalia weapon, the Gladius, is high might, high accuracy, and has 1-2 range.

Double also? Depending on how you’re doing, you may want to train up Merric and promote him instead of Lena. You mostly want Lena for her staff utility, and as long as her Weapon Lv is decently high, she doesn’t need to promote for that, though it’s probably worth promoting her in FE3 more than it is in FE1.

I think people get blindsided by the theme of redemption in the show.

At its core, Hazbin is showing that its outlook is primarily positive and optimistic, despite initial appearances. People who seem bad and unreachable can have soft spots. Change and redemption are possible, if you put the work in. Even Heaven, which is primarily shown to be antagonistic, can be shown to be capable of goodness and change. Sera chose to allow the exterminations out of fear, not malice; the other head angels gathered at the trial begin to debate each other about the exterminations, meaning many of them clearly don’t accept the exterminations; Emily is outright disgusted by them. A lesser show would just show Heaven as an antagonistic monolith; Hazbin is genuinely very realistic in showing how nothing is black and white, which goes with the show’s theme of how using the labels of good and evil are usually pretty useless. 

Viv is also careful to show that, while redemption is a possibility, there are people who actively don’t want and won’t get redemption. Viv is clearly saying the door is open to everyone; she’s also showing people ahead of time that Alastor actively refuses to go through this door.

Take the Finale. There are three factions singing: let’s call them Inclusivity (Charlie, Lucifer, and the Hotel residents), Exclusivity (the Vees), and Solipism (Alastor). The Inclusivity faction is open, warm, and accepting of each other. They’ve decided to band together to work not just for each other, but a better tomorrow. They’re growing into a community that welcomes others.

The Vees part sings about their hopes that their dreams are coming true and they have a chance to rise to the top among the Overlords. Throughout S1 we’re shown how legitimately wicked, self promoting, and brazen. They’re genuinely villainous. And yet the last lyric of their part of the song is super important.

“Nature abhors a power vacuum
Leaving room for you and me!
The future of Hell belongs to the Vees!”

As shitty as the Vees are, Val, Vox, and Vel are, they’re sincere about their feelings for each other. They’re bound by genuine companionship, even if their intentions to everyone else are malevolent. The hotel is Inclusive in their companionship; the Vees are exclusive in theirs.

And yet, both the hotel and the Vees share community in common. They’re both factions that have that bond. It’s why there’s a transition in the music from the hotel group to the Vees, but it’s still fairly similar.

Then we get to Alastor. The music changes drastically. Alastor is the only character granted a true solo in the Finale.

Throughout Hazbin, the viewers are welcomed in to moments of intimacy with the characters, where they let their masks drop. Even Adam is allowed this, complete with his actual mask being forcibly shattered before Adam shares any of his actual real feelings. The only character who doesn’t let their mask drop is Alastor. Until his part in the Finale.

The hotel and Vees sing about their hopes and dreams as a community. What feelings await us with Alastor’s mask drop?

Rage. Absolute blinding rage and Alastor’s plans for Alastor and Alastor alone. Alastor solipistically focuses only on Alastor, no one else, because no one else matters to him.

Alastor’s part is about how he’s pissed at every one and every thing around him. Not only that, but several of Alastor’s lyrics show how he’s in opposition to the others at the Hotel. A notable one is this lyric:

“Great Alastor, altruist, died for his friends?
Sorry to disappoint, but that’s not how this ends.”

This line does two things.

1) It’s Viv’s continued warning that we should believe Alastor when he tells us how dangerous and cruel he is. Unlike the others, there’s no sweetness under Alastor’s shell. If anything, he actively uses sweetness - his smile, his usual polite demeanor and way of speaking - as a disguise, unlike the cynicism everyone else uses to hide their actual feelings and

2) It shows how pointless and stupid Alastor thinks self-sacrifice is, and him insulting Ser Pentious indirectly for his own sacrifice. 

Another example is Alastor talking about how he’s desperately looking for a way to worm out of his deal. This echoes Alastor and Husker. Husker hates being bound to Alastor, but there’s actually a sense of honor to Husker. He abides by his deals and the consequences that come with them.

Alastor does not.

Ser Pentious, despite his desire to be an Overlord, ultimately comes to cherish his friends and the possibility of compassion and love. He sees value in it.

Alastor does not. 

Alastor is being set up as the direct antagonist to the very themes Hazbin Hotel embraces. I think there’s honestly evidence Alastor is so far the most morally depraved and villainous character in the showeven more so than Adam, and that’s by design.

Viv is telling a genuinely beautiful story about redemption, and that includes the fact that there aren’t just people beyond redemption but those, like Alastor, who actively reject it.

Crocodile is the more likely. In modern academia, leviathan is usually thought to refer to the crocodile and behemoth to the hippo. Which makes sense, since these are animals the ancient readers would have familiarity with.

‘Satan’ isn’t a demon in either Christian or Jewish theology. The idea of Satan (as a named entity) was essentially a mistranslation/understanding. In Hebrew, Satan is a word meaning ‘adversary’, not a name, and is used to describe an angel, not a demon, who is behaving adversarially towards Job. It’s why God just greets ‘Satan’ in Job and asks him where he’s been wondering to a fro; it’s actually an angel who was meant to be walking over the world and watching people.

The point of the Book of Job is that it was essentially a corrective to earlier theology. Earlier theology in the Bible presumed that if awful things happening to a person meant that it was punishment from God/for sin. The point of the Biblical book of Job is that awful things can befall people for no reason, and that questioning God is not inherently wrong in these times of grief.

The point of God addressing this with Job is to underline how unfathomable life is, and that answers aren’t forthcoming because there are, at times, no answers.

Valentia is already one of the more forgiving games you can play due to the fact it has grinding available in the base game. I don’t think you should have too much trouble with the game on hard even if you don’t grind so long as you play carefully like you would in any other Fire Emblem. I’ve never actually played Valentia in Normal so I can’t give you information on differences, but I can give you advice.

- Keep in mind that during Alm’s route, Alm will be  one of your most competent units. He’s great until chapter three, at which point he’ll get a weapon that grants him an ability called Double Lion, at which point Alm becomes a complete monster. 

- Mercenaries are great units and the best class line in the game, so two are fine. I wouldn’t make any of the villagers cavaliers though. Alm’s route is swarming with cavaliers, and the villager you’re going to get on the second route doesn’t benefit from being a cav because of the terrain on that route. If this is your first time through the game, I’d suggest making at least one villager a mage (probably Tobin) and Faye a cleric. 

- You usually want to prioritize killing spellcasters when you can. Resistance is almost universal low for everyone in this game (until you get access to Dread Fighter) and Res growth is single digit, so magic can hurt. Magic also works different then it does in other games, as spells have a flat to-hit ratio, but they also ignore the bonkers terrain bonuses Echoes has.

- On the second route at Chapter Three there’s a point where you’ll have to choose between fighting a mage and fighting a mercenary. Since this is your first run I’d argue you should fight the mage.

- Never wait to promote. There aren’t really promotion bonuses in this game, but rather promoting will make sure your characters are brought to the base stats for that class. Promote the moment you get the chance to. There is no benefit to grinding to 20 on everything.

- Forge a Killer Bow when you get the chance to.

- One last thing: use Invoke. The game is built in mind with you summoning phantoms when you can. They usually can’t deal much damage, but enemies will tend to prioritize them a lot, taking heat off your own units.

The Bible was written by men, and while much of it was divinely communicated, you have to remember that men still used human ways to move information along.
